name: Analytic vs. synthetic and a priori vs. empirical propositions
plain_explanation: An analytic proposition is true just by the meaning of its words ('a tall man is a man'); a synthetic one adds real information ('Napoleon was a great general'). Separately, an empirical proposition can only be known through sense experience ('Tuesday was a wet day'); an a priori one, though perhaps triggered by experience, is seen to hold with a certainty experience alone could never give (like '2+2=4').
precise_definition: Kant separates two distinctions that Leibniz had run together: analytic (predicate contained in the subject, governed by the law of contradiction) versus synthetic (predicate not so contained), and a priori (known independently of, though perhaps occasioned by, experience) versus empirical (knowable only via sense-perception or testimony).
why_it_mattered: It lets Kant formulate the central problem of the Critique of Pure Reason: since Hume showed causality is not analytic, and Kant holds mathematics and causality are nonetheless a priori, he must explain how synthetic a priori knowledge -- knowledge that is both informative and yet certain independent of experience -- is possible at all.
historical_origin: Critique of Pure Reason (1st ed. 1781, 2nd ed. 1787).
examples: 'Two and two are four' (synthetic, a priori, per Kant)
The propositions of pure mathematics, held by Kant to be synthetic a priori
competing_positions: Leibniz's view, which Kant rejects, that all synthetic propositions are known only through experience
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became the organizing question for the whole Critique of Pure Reason and for subsequent German idealism.
